findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a legal IEnumerable such as `attrs.Where(a => a.Type != typeof(CompilerGeneratedAttribute))`, a HashSet<AttributeStatement>, or a yield iterator to `new ParameterProvider(..., attributes: ...)` or `parameter.Update(attributes: ...)`. The `as` cast returns null and the expression evaluates to `[]`, so the attributes vanish and the generated method parameter is emitted without them (e.g., a wire-format marker attribute is silently dropped) with no exception and no compile error. Before this change the parameter was typed `IReadOnlyList<AttributeStatement>` so such input could not even be passed; the PR's type widening introduced the silent data loss (line 303 has the same defect in Update).
findings.summary: ParameterProvider's constructor and Update widened `attributes` from IReadOnlyList to IEnumerable but silently discard any enumerable that is not an IReadOnlyList via `(attributes as IReadOnlyList<AttributeStatement>) ?? []`.

findings.failure_scenario: A generator plugin calls `new MethodProvider(sig, body, type, attributes: attrs.Where(a => ...))` or passes a HashSet or iterator; the cast yields null and `[]` is stored, so attributes such as `[Obsolete]` never appear in the generated code even though the accepted `IEnumerable<AttributeStatement>` parameter makes the input legal. Same defect at MethodProvider.Update (line 106), ConstructorProvider ctors (lines 51/73), PropertyProvider ctor/Update (lines 127/303), and FieldProvider ctor/Update (lines 69/130). ConstructorProvider.Update (line 105) and TypeProvider.Update (line 465) correctly use `[.. attributes]`, proving the drop pattern is unintended.
findings.summary: The new `attributes` parameters on MethodProvider/ConstructorProvider/PropertyProvider/FieldProvider constructors and Update methods use `(attributes as IReadOnlyList<AttributeStatement>) ?? []`, silently dropping any enumerable that is not an IReadOnlyList.

findings.failure_scenario: LibraryVisitor.VisitLibrary calls type.EnsureBuilt() (LibraryVisitor.cs:23) before visitors run, which materializes field.AsParameter while building constructors (ModelProvider.cs:619/624). A visitor then calls `field.Update(attributes: [new AttributeStatement(typeof(ObsoleteAttribute))])` or `field.Update(type: newType)`: the field itself is updated and WriteField emits the attribute, but the already-created ParameterProvider still holds the old empty attributes or old type (including stale null-validation computed from the old type), so the generated constructor parameter lacks the attribute or keeps a type that mismatches the field, producing wrong or non-compiling generated code. The name branch (line 104) explicitly re-creates the lazy, showing propagation is required and intended; the other branches omit it.
findings.summary: FieldProvider.Update does not re-initialize the `_parameter` Lazy when type, description, wireInfo, or attributes change (only the name branch does), so updates made after `AsParameter` was materialized silently never reach the constructor parameter.

findings.failure_scenario: The same generated method now has two independent attribute lists (signature-level and provider-level), both emitted at different points in CodeWriter, that must be kept in sync manually: `method.Update(signature: newSig)` does not reconcile Attributes, and visitors using the pre-existing `signature.Update(attributes: ...)` path bypass the new property entirely. Attributes set via one path are invisible to code that reads the other (custom-code matching, canonical-view consumers, tests), creating redundant derivable state instead of extending the existing MethodSignatureBase/ConstructorSignature mechanism — the new collection should have been routed through the signature attributes.
findings.summary: MethodProvider and ConstructorProvider gain a second, parallel Attributes collection even though MethodSignatureBase.Attributes already models method attributes and CodeWriter.WriteMethodDeclarationNoScope (line 765) already emits them.

findings.failure_scenario: Downstream code compiled against the old signature calling `type.Update(methods, ctors, props, fields, serializations, nestedTypes, xmlDocs, modifiers)` now binds xmlDocs to `attributes` and modifiers to `xmlDocs`: a compile error when non-null (XmlDocProvider is not IEnumerable<AttributeStatement>), or a silent loss of the intended xml-docs/modifiers updates when nulls were passed positionally. The only in-repo positional caller (LibraryVisitor.cs:103, six args) is unaffected, but external generator plugins break. Appending `attributes` after `xmlDocs` (as done in MethodProvider.Update and PropertyProvider.Update) avoids the rebinding.
findings.summary: TypeProvider.Update inserts the new optional `attributes` parameter before `xmlDocs` in the parameter list, rebinding every positional argument from position 7 onward for callers of this public API.

findings.failure_scenario: No symbol from System.Reflection.Metadata is referenced anywhere in the file (only the using line matches), so the leftover directive adds build/IDE0005 noise and misleads readers about the change's dependencies. Maintainability cost only; it suggests the edit was intended for a different file.
findings.summary: Unused `using System.Reflection.Metadata;` was added to CodeWriter.cs.
